# Discord Is Not a Community Strategy. Neither Is Telegram.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/discord-telegram-community-strategy/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-05 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Growth

> Summary: Opening a Discord or Telegram makes a Web3 project feel operational before the relationships and operating system exist. Start from the jobs members need done, build the smallest set of spaces that serves them, treat moderation and security messaging as product design, and move durable knowledge out of chat. Choose the platform after the behaviour.

A Discord server or Telegram group is infrastructure, not a strategy. Start from the jobs members need done, decide which need real-time chat and which need durable documentation, and build the smallest set of spaces that serves them. In crypto, safety is part of the design: the FBI recorded $11.4 billion in crypto-related fraud losses in 2025, and a chat full of impersonators is where much of it starts. Choose the platform after the behaviour.

Opening a Discord or Telegram is one of the fastest ways for a Web3 project to feel operational. There are channels, roles, moderators, bots, announcements and a visible member count. The interface resembles a community before the relationships and operating system exist.

The result is often a familiar pattern: dozens of empty channels, repeated support questions, speculative price conversation, scam attempts, overwhelmed moderators, and a small number of genuine contributors buried beneath noise. Our piece [40,000 members and nobody does anything](https://lowob.com/research/40-000-members-and-nobody-does-anything/) describes where that ends. This playbook is part of our hub on [building a community that lasts](https://lowob.com/research/building-a-community-that-lasts/).

## Begin with jobs, not channels

List the jobs members need the environment to perform, then decide where each belongs. Real-time chat is good at some of them and bad at most.

| Member job | Best home | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Receive authoritative announcements | Read-only channel, mirrored to email and the website | Needs one canonical source that cannot be spoofed in replies |
| Get product or wallet support | Structured help channel or ticket | Sensitive details should not sit in public chat |
| Learn how the protocol works | Searchable documentation and FAQ | Durable answers should not scroll away |
| Meet collaborators | Discussion space, events, smaller groups | Needs real-time conversation and repeat contact |
| Give structured feedback | Forum or form with an owner | Needs to be counted and answered |
| Contribute code, research, governance or content | Briefs, working groups, a governance forum | Needs a durable record and recognition |
| Discuss the market | One clearly labelled channel | Keeps speculation away from official guidance |

An FAQ belongs in searchable documentation. A sensitive support issue belongs in a ticket. A product workshop may belong on a call. A governance proposal needs a durable forum. A critical announcement needs a canonical home, even if it is distributed through chat.

## Design the minimum viable architecture

For an early project, a small number of clearly differentiated spaces usually works better than a sprawling structure:

- **Start here:** orientation, rules, security warnings, official links and how to get help.
- **Announcements:** read-only updates with clear source authority.
- **Help:** structured questions with searchable answers and escalation rules.
- **Discussion:** one or two spaces tied to the project's main member interests.
- **Contribute:** specific opportunities, briefs, working groups and recognition.
- **Events:** schedule, preparation, notes and follow-up.

Create additional channels only when repeated behaviour justifies them. Empty segmentation makes the community look less active and raises navigation cost.

Both platforms now have native tools for this. Discord's Community Onboarding lets members answer questions that assign them roles and channels; Discord requires at least seven default channels, at least five of which everyone can view and post in, so the minimum architecture above fits the tool. Telegram added Topics in November 2022, which turn a large group into separate threads with their own media and notification settings, and admins control who can create them. Telegram's own FAQ draws the line between its two formats: groups, up to 200,000 members, are for collaboration; channels, with unlimited subscribers, are "a tool for broadcasting messages to large audiences". Use a channel for announcements and a group with Topics for conversation, rather than one group doing both.

## Build a visible member journey

A new member should immediately understand where they are, whether it is official and safe, what is valuable here, what to do first, who can help and how to contribute.

The first meaningful action should be more useful than posting an introduction nobody reads. Ask members to select a relevant path, attend a recurring session, answer a focused question or use a starter resource. Discord's onboarding questions can route a developer, a user and a liquidity provider to different starting channels on day one. Our guide to the [first 100 community members](https://lowob.com/research/first-100-community-members/) covers who those first members should be.

## Treat moderation and security as product design

Moderation is not merely deleting spam. It defines the behaviour the environment rewards.

Publish rules that address scams, impersonation, harassment, price discussion, unsolicited promotion, direct-message safety, disclosure and enforcement. Give moderators documented escalation paths. Discord's guidance recommends letting automation handle routine issues around the clock while recognising that "not every violation will have a simple solution", and keeping enforcement "as fair and consistent as possible". Its AutoMod tool supports custom keyword rules of up to 1,000 terms, a spam content filter, a cap on mentions per message and alerts to a private moderator channel. Use those for repeatable protection and keep humans responsible for context.

In Web3, security communication should be repetitive by design. The stakes are measurable. The FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report recorded $11.366 billion in crypto-related losses across 181,565 complaints, with crypto investment fraud alone at $7.2 billion. Chainalysis estimated more than $3.4 billion was stolen in crypto hacks in 2025, with personal wallet compromises accounting for 20% of value stolen. Not all of that starts in a community chat, but impersonated admins, fake support DMs and spoofed links are a common entry point.

So state, in the start-here space and in every announcement that matters: where official announcements appear, that team members will never initiate direct messages, how wallet links are verified and how incidents are reported. Telegram's own FAQ models the tone: it says it has no other support accounts on social platforms, and that anyone elsewhere claiming to be Telegram is not.

> In a crypto community, the security message is not a one-time rule. It is the most repeated sentence the project publishes.

## Prevent knowledge from disappearing into chat

Real-time conversation creates information and then rapidly buries it. Every week, extract recurring questions, unresolved product confusion, valuable member answers, feature requests, emerging risks or rumours, decisions from working sessions and resources worth preserving.

Move durable knowledge into documentation, an FAQ, a forum or the project's public playbooks, and link back to the canonical answer. Discord's own guidance suggests a read-only FAQ channel members are pointed to before they ask. This reduces repeated work and turns community activity into organisational knowledge. The same principle runs through our playbook on [content with a job](https://lowob.com/research/content-with-a-job/): a durable answer needs an owner and a review date, or it drifts from the product.

## Measure whether the environment creates value

Useful measures include time to first useful response, percentage of questions resolved, repeat participation by cohort, member-to-member help, unique contributors, movement into product use or contribution, safety incidents and response time, and recurring questions eliminated through better documentation.

Message volume can indicate engagement or confusion. Context determines which. A spike in the help channel after a release is a product signal, not a community win.

## Choose the platform after the behaviour

Telegram may suit fast-moving announcements and lightweight conversation. Discord may better support structured roles, onboarding, topic areas, events and moderation. Forums and documentation are better for durable knowledge. Email reaches people who will not monitor another chat. Smaller private groups may produce more trust than one public server.

The right answer is often a simple system across several surfaces, each with a defined job. Our [build order for crypto and digital assets](https://lowob.com/research/the-build-order-for-crypto-and-digital-assets/) makes the same point for the commercial side: write down which system holds which record before adding tools.

## lowob takeaways

- **Jobs before channels.** List what members need done, then give each job a home.
- **Small and differentiated.** About six spaces for an early project; add channels only when behaviour demands them.
- **Security is repetitive by design.** State where announcements live, that the team never DMs first, and how to report incidents.
- **Extract weekly.** Move durable answers out of chat into documentation and link back.

## Next move

List the jobs your members need done this week and give each one a home. Archive any channel that has had no meaningful activity in 30 days, and pin a three-line security notice at the top of the start-here space.
